Multi-asset research note

Statistical Learning and Macro Portfolio Allocation

Macro-quantamental information has a plausible bearing on the returns of all major asset classes. Applied to the allocation of capital across eleven asset classes and cash, theory-guided macro themes have produced a higher Sharpe ratio than equal weights and a much lower dependence on equity markets. Sequential statistical learning on the same factors has slightly improved on equal weights, with a similar reduction in equity exposure.

Data: FRED, BIS, OECD, Eurostat, ECB, EIA and Yahoo FinanceUniverse: 11 asset classes plus cash, October 2004 – October 2026Signals: 36 macro themes and a 35-model learning ensemble
SummaryThe basic ideaThe dataTheory-guided signalLearning-based signalValue checksConsistencyAnnex

Summary

Asset class allocation is a core decision in multi-asset portfolios, and macroeconomic conditions plausibly inform it. Excess inflation weighs on bonds, growth above trend supports equities, and rate differentials pay currency carry. This study translates public macro data into allocation weights for eleven asset classes in two ways. A theory-guided signal combines 36 macro themes with signs set by economic reasoning. A learning-based signal comes from an ensemble of 35 regression models that sequentially select and weight 74 macro factors for each asset class. Both signals are converted into weights by the same softmax rule, with cash as an alternative.

Both macro allocations have produced value against an equal-weight benchmark. Since October 2004 the theory-guided allocation has posted a Sharpe ratio of 0.61, against 0.53 for the learning-based allocation and 0.52 for equal weights. Statistical learning has thus been a slight improvement on equal weights, with marginally higher risk-adjusted and compounded returns and the smallest drawdown. Both macro allocations have reduced the correlation with US equities from 0.77 to about 0.58. The return advantage has been concentrated in the years before 2010. Since mid-2010 the theory-guided allocation has matched equal weights on Sharpe ratio, which makes lower equity dependence its most consistent contribution.

The basic idea

A multi-asset portfolio holds equities, government bonds, credit, currencies and commodities. Each asset class depends on the economy in its own way. Inflation above target has historically been negative for bonds, growth above trend positive for equities, and high relative interest rates supportive for currencies. Since such conditions change gradually and are observable, they should help allocate capital across asset classes.

The simplest benchmark ignores this information and splits capital equally. However, equities from different regions move together and are more volatile than most other asset classes, so an equal split is dominated by equity risk. Macro signals can tilt the allocation towards asset classes supported by economic conditions and away from those that are not.

The process runs from raw data to portfolio weights in seven stages.

  1. Targets. Each asset class is represented by a daily USD excess return, the return over cash.
  2. Macro factors. Country series are transformed into factors such as excess inflation, growth relative to trend, real rates, credit growth, carry and survey levels, each lagged by its publication delay.
  3. Geographic composites. Factors are averaged across countries with GDP weights into global, developed, emerging and asset-class baskets.
  4. Scores. Each composite is normalized against its own history with zero-neutral z-scores, so that factors in different units become comparable.
  5. Theory-guided signal. Scores are combined into macro themes, and themes into one support score per asset class.
  6. Learning-based signal. For each asset class, an ensemble of regression models learns which factors have predicted next month's return, with quarterly re-estimation on data available at the time.
  7. Allocation. Either signal is translated into weights through a softmax rule that includes cash, with quarterly rebalancing.

The data

Asset class returns

All eleven asset classes are measured as daily USD excess returns over the federal funds rate. US Treasuries are a constant-maturity 5-year bond priced from the daily yield, and US credit adds Baa spread carry and spread changes to that bond. Developed FX is a basket of nine currency forwards against the dollar. Developed and emerging equities are baskets of country ETFs, and the remaining six asset classes use one ETF each. The chart below shows the period over which each return series is available.

Each bar runs from the first available return to October 2026. Treasuries, US credit and developed FX reach back to 1990, and the two equity baskets to 1996. Developed government bonds, emerging hard-currency debt and industrial metals start only in 2007, and emerging local-currency bonds in July 2010. Before those dates the allocation can only choose among fewer asset classes, which is why performance is also checked from July 2010 onward. An asset class receives no weight before its first trading day.

The chart below positions each asset class by its correlation with US equities and its own Sharpe ratio since October 2004.

The horizontal axis measures how closely each asset class has moved with US equities, and the vertical axis its own return per unit of risk. Developed and emerging equities have correlated 0.88 and 0.83 with US equities, so three of eleven asset classes have effectively represented one market. Since equities are also among the more volatile asset classes, they dominate the risk of an equal split. Credit, gold and US Treasuries sit near or below zero correlation and are the main diversifiers. Standalone Sharpe ratios have ranged from −0.08 for developed government bonds to 0.78 for US credit, so no fixed split would have suited all periods.

Macro factors

Country series from BIS, OECD, Eurostat, ECB and FRED are transformed into 55 factor categories across 36 economies with fixed formulas, each lagged by its typical publication delay. The chart below shows how many economies each multi-country category covers.

Exchange-rate, house-price, credit, carry and survey factors cover 23 to 36 economies, so global and regional composites rest on broad samples. Growth, labor and industrial factors cover only 14 economies, as only Eurostat and FRED supply local histories. A further 28 categories, such as Treasury yields, bank lending surveys, inflation expectations and housing starts, exist for the US alone. Composites therefore lean towards the US economy where broader data are missing. Factors are averaged into composites with nominal GDP weights applied 18 months after year-end, and emerging-market observations before 1996 are excluded to keep hyperinflation values from distorting the scoring scale.

Macro inputs are revised histories shifted by approximate publication lags rather than point-in-time vintages, so backtests overstate what was knowable in real time. Equity carry, commodity carry, metal inventories, sovereign CDS spreads and terms of trade are not available from free daily sources and are missing from the factor set.

Theory-guided signal

Theory-guided signals combine factors into 36 themes that each represent one economic concept, such as demand, inflation, labor market tightness, financial conditions or currency carry. Each asset class is assigned a list of themes with signs set by economic reasoning. Strong demand enters equities with a positive sign, and high inflation enters duration with a negative sign. The chart below shows how many themes support each asset class.

US credit draws on nine themes and developed government bonds on eight, so their support scores average many independent economic views. Industrial metals rest on two themes and developed FX and gold on three, so their scores depend on fewer inputs and can swing more on a single theme. Themes are averaged and re-scored into one support score per asset class. The chart below shows these support scores over time.

Each panel shows one asset class, with positive values meaning the economy supports it and the grey line marking neutral. Treasury and developed-bond scores rose to the +3 cap in 2008–09 and fell to −3 in 2022, matching the swing from crisis easing to post-pandemic inflation. Credit scores stayed at the cap through the 2009 recovery. Equity scores spiked in 2020–21 and US equities then held at −3 through 2023. Industrial metals scored highest in 2021–22. The scores rotate across asset classes rather than moving together, which is what an allocation signal needs.

Quarter-end support scores are compared with next-quarter excess returns, pooled across asset classes, as shown below.

Each dot is one asset class in one quarter, with the support score at quarter-end on the horizontal axis and the following quarter's excess return on the vertical axis. The red regression line rises from about 0% at a score of −3 to about 2% at +3. The Pearson correlation has been 0.068 and the Kendall rank correlation 0.059, with probabilities of significance of 96% and above 99%. The stronger rank result indicates that the relation does not depend on a few extreme quarters. This is a typical magnitude for macro signals, whose value arises from many decisions across asset classes and years rather than from individual calls.

Learning-based signal

The learning-based signal selects predictors without prior judgement on their direction. For each asset class, 35 models use all 74 scored factors at month-end to predict next month's return, scaled to 10% annualized volatility. Each model first condenses the factors into 5 to 10 principal components and then applies Ridge, Lasso, time-weighted least squares or OLS regression. Models are re-estimated every quarter with data available at the time, once 48 months of history exist. The forecast averages all models, weighted by their accuracy over three expanding validation periods, and the largest model weight has averaged only about 0.045.

Both signals are translated into weights by the same softmax rule. Each asset class receives a weight proportional to the exponential of its score, with cash competing at a score of zero. The chart below shows the resulting weights over time.

Each colour band is one asset class, and the bands stack to 100% of capital. The theory-guided allocation shifted towards emerging equities in 2005–07, towards credit after 2009 and towards metals in 2021–23, and reduced US equity exposure in 2008 and 2022. The learning-based allocation has rotated more frequently and held more duration and FX in its early years, when fewer asset classes traded. Neither allocation concentrates in one asset class for long, since the softmax rule softens differences between scores.

The chart below shows the correlation of monthly out-of-sample forecasts with subsequent returns, and the table compares forecast errors with those of a zero forecast.

Blue bars are positive correlations and the orange bar the one negative. Ten of eleven forecasts have been positively correlated with subsequent returns, led by developed FX at 0.095 and US equities at 0.087. Emerging local-currency bonds, with the shortest history of 138 months, are the exception at −0.091. No forecast has beaten a zero forecast on squared error, as forecast variation has been large relative to the predictive edge. This matters less for allocation, since weights are based on re-scored signals and the raw size of each forecast drops out.

Value checks

Naive PnL

Naive PnLs apply the weights to excess returns with quarterly rebalancing and a one-day slippage between signal and position. They exclude transaction costs and risk management and therefore measure the signal itself. The benchmark is an equal allocation across live asset classes and cash. The chart below shows cumulative PnL in percent of risk capital, without compounding.

In this chart PNL_MACRO is the theory-guided allocation, PNL_ML the learning-based allocation and PNL_EQUAL equal weights. The theory-guided allocation built a lead of about 30 points by 2008 and ended near 125%, against about 100% for the other two. The learning-based allocation lagged in 2005–08, overtook equal weights after 2016 and has stayed slightly ahead since. All three fell in the 2008, 2020 and 2022 sell-offs, but the equal-weight PnL dropped hardest in late 2008, close to its starting level. The chart below compares correlations with US equities.

Both macro allocations have had correlations of about 0.58 with US equities, against 0.77 for equal weights, consistent with the lower equity weights in 2008 and 2022. A correlation of 0.58 still leaves equities as a major driver, but a materially smaller one. Both macro allocations have taken over four years to recover from their largest drawdown, against 16 months for equal weights, since a tilt away from equities also reduces participation in the subsequent recovery. The chart below compares losses over three horizons.

Shorter bars mean smaller losses. The learning-based allocation has had the smallest loss on all three measures, at −18.4% over 21 days, −28.5% over six months and −29.1% peak to trough. Equal weights have lost most on all three, including −22.1% in the worst month. The theory-guided allocation matches the learning-based one over 21 days but sits close to equal weights on longer horizons. Lower drawdowns are a main part of the slight improvement that statistical learning has offered over equal weights.

Wealth generation with compounding

Total returns add back the cash rate and compound daily, with month-end weights applied from the next session. The chart below shows the growth of one dollar since January 2004.

In the chart, Economic control is the theory-guided allocation and Equal capital is equal weights. The log scale makes equal percentage moves equal in height. One dollar invested in January 2004 has grown to about $4.70 in the theory-guided allocation and to between $3.50 and $3.70 in the other two. The theory-guided allocation has compounded at 6.9% a year, against 5.8% for the learning-based allocation and 5.6% for equal weights, and established most of its lead by 2008. The learning-based allocation has slightly improved on equal weights in wealth terms and has had the smallest maximum drawdown, at −21% against −27% and −28%.

Consistency of the value-add

Performance is compared over the full sample and over the period since July 2010, when all eleven asset classes trade.

Over the full sample the theory-guided allocation has led equal weights by 0.09 Sharpe points, and the learning-based allocation has improved slightly on equal weights, at 0.53 against 0.52. Since mid-2010 the theory-guided allocation and equal weights have both posted 0.47, while the learning-based allocation has been marginally lower at 0.44 despite a higher annual return of 3.98% against 3.62%. The theory-guided allocation has still earned 0.4 percentage points more per year since 2010, but with higher volatility. Most of the risk-adjusted return advantage has thus accrued between 2004 and 2010, a period that includes the global financial crisis and fewer live asset classes.

The chart below shows the probability that each allocation's true Sharpe ratio exceeds three thresholds, given the length and noise of its track record.

All three allocations have a true Sharpe ratio above 0.25 with probability above 99%. The theory-guided allocation has a 93% probability of exceeding 0.5 and 46% of exceeding 0.75, against 82% and 27% for equal weights. The learning-based and equal-weight allocations have nearly identical probabilities, so the slight improvement from statistical learning lies within the statistical uncertainty of a 22-year record. The theory-guided allocation is the only one with a clearly higher chance of a strong Sharpe ratio.

Data and method. FRED, EIA and Yahoo Finance series pulled through public APIs, plus BIS, OECD, Eurostat and ECB country exports. Eleven asset classes in USD excess returns; macro factors lagged by publication delay and averaged with GDP weights; theory-guided signal from 36 themes; learning-based signal from a 35-model PCA regression ensemble re-estimated quarterly. Weights by softmax with cash, quarterly rebalancing, one-day slippage, no costs. Macro inputs are revised histories rather than point-in-time vintages.
